title: Eastern Air Lines 21
summary: Eastern Air Lines Flight 21, a Douglas DC-3, crashed on February 26, 1941 while preparing to land at Candler Field near Atlanta, killing eight of sixteen occupants including Congressman William Byron. The aircraft struck the tops of three small pine trees at 915 feet elevation while flying northerly. Investigation found the instrument approach altimeter was set to 29.92 inches of mercury when Candler Field setting was 28.94, an error of exactly one inch corresponding to the altitude error that caused descent below safe approach altitude.
probable_cause: The instrument approach altimeter apparently had been set incorrectly to 29.92 inches of mercury when the correct altimeter setting at Candler Field was 28.94, causing the aircraft to descend below safe altitude during instrument approach.

the altimeter setting could have been disturbed in the crash, but the error in the setting was almost exactly one inch of mercury

events.text: Flight 21 departed LaGuardia Airport on the evening of February 26, stopped briefly at Washington-Hoover Airport before departing at 9:05 PM Eastern Time for Atlanta.
The aircraft called the Eastern Air Lines operator in Atlanta to advise that it had passed over the Stone Mountain reporting point and was descending.

Flight 21 contacted the Atlanta control tower twice, first to advise that it was making an approach and then to advise that the aircraft was over the Atlanta range station two miles southeast of the airport at an altitude of 1800 ft.
The company operator suggested a straight-in approach and the aircraft acknowledged the transmission, but nothing further was heard.

The aircraft had first struck the tops of three small pine trees while flying northerly, then continued across a small valley in level flight for about 1500 feet before the right wing struck the top of a poplar and the aircraft crashed into a thick grove of pine trees five miles southeast of Atlanta.
